scenes.headline: Performance Profiling & Optimization
scenes.subtitle: Measure first, then optimize
scenes.narration: Performance work begins with measurement, because the golden rule of optimization is that you cannot fix what you have not first proven to be slow.

scenes.headline: Why profile before optimizing
items: Intuition about bottlenecks is frequently wrong
The 80/20 rule: most time hides in a few hot spots
Premature optimization wastes effort and adds complexity
scenes.narration: Engineers routinely guess wrong about where their code spends its time, optimizing a function that barely matters while the real cost hides elsewhere. In practice, the overwhelming majority of runtime concentrates in a handful of hot spots. Profiling reveals exactly where those are, so you spend your effort where it pays off instead of adding complexity for imaginary gains.

scenes.headline: Profiling tools by scope
scenes.narration: Different tools answer different questions. cProfile is the standard-library workhorse that reports how often each function is called and how much cumulative time it consumes, giving you a program-wide map. Once cProfile points at a suspect function, line_profiler zooms in to show the time spent on each individual line inside it. Start broad with cProfile, then narrow with line_profiler on the hot function.

scenes.headline: Profiling with cProfile
scenes.code:
import cProfile
import pstats

profiler = cProfile.Profile()
profiler.enable()

run_pipeline(data)

profiler.disable()
stats = pstats.Stats(profiler)
stats.sort_stats("cumulative").print_stats(10)
scenes.narration: Here a cProfile.Profile object records everything between enable and disable. After the pipeline runs, the collected data is wrapped in a Stats object for analysis. Sorting by cumulative time and printing the top ten immediately surfaces the functions responsible for the most total runtime, giving you a ranked list of where to look first.

scenes.headline: Common optimizations
items: Vectorize with NumPy or pandas instead of Python loops
Choose the right data structure, like a set for membership tests
Push heavy work down to C libraries or the database
scenes.narration: Once you know the hot spot, the highest-leverage fix in data work is usually vectorization, replacing slow per-row Python loops with NumPy or pandas operations that run in C. Picking the right data structure matters too, since a set turns a linear membership test into a constant-time one. Caching repeated computations with lru_cache eliminates redundant work, and offloading heavy lifting to native libraries or the database often beats any Python-level tuning.

scenes.headline: The optimization loop
scenes.narration: Effective optimization is a disciplined loop rather than a burst of guessing. You measure to find the biggest bottleneck, apply a single targeted change, and then measure again to confirm it actually helped. Repeating that cycle keeps every change grounded in evidence and stops you from optimizing things that never mattered.

scenes.text: Profile first, fix the biggest hot spot, then re-measure — optimize with evidence, never with guesses.
scenes.narration: Let data, not intuition, drive your performance work: profile first, attack the largest hot spot, and verify the gain by measuring again. Evidence-based optimization is faster to write and far more effective.
